_comment: Site-card language. Owner: Julia (task J5). Eduard's placeholder so the UI renders; Julia rewrites every string, Sofia reviews the science and Finn the construction lines. {site} and {target} are substituted by the UI. Keep each line under 30 words.

T.why: Terrain decides where a lander can touch down and where a rover can drive.
T.strong: Slopes and roughness at {site} sit inside the range measured at {target}.
T.partial: Broad landforms match {target}, but the fine roughness differs.
T.breaks: The ground at {site} is a different shape from {target} - expect different mobility behaviour.

H.why: Thermal inertia tells you how loose or rocky the surface is, and temperature sets the engineering envelope.
H.strong: Surface material at {site} responds to heating much like {target}.
H.partial: Similar material class, different absolute temperatures.
H.breaks: Temperatures and surface response at {site} are nothing like {target}.

M.why: Rock type and albedo drive instrument response, sample science and dust behaviour.
M.partial: Related rock types, but not the same family.
M.breaks: Different rock chemistry from {target} - mineralogy tests will not transfer.

W.why: Where water ice sits, and how dry the place is, drives ISRU and biosignature work.
W.strong: Ice presence and dryness at {site} are close to {target}.
W.partial: Dry, but not as dry as {target} - or ice is present in a different form.
W.breaks: Water behaves completely differently here than at {target}.

B.why: Life changes soil chemistry and contaminates biosignature tests.
B.partial: Sparse vegetation - usable, but biology is present.
B.breaks: This is a living landscape; {target} is not.

C.why: Buildability decides whether a permanent base can be founded, excavated and landed on at all.
C.strong: Flat, firm ground at {site} matches what a builder would face at {target}.
C.partial: Buildable in places, but the ground differs from {target} in firmness or flatness.
C.breaks: This ground could not stand in for {target}: the slopes or the soil behave differently.

A.why: Dust loading and wind shape visibility, solar power and equipment wear.
A.strong: Dust and wind regime comparable to {target}.
A.partial: Dusty, but the particle transport regime differs.
A.breaks: Atmospheric conditions here do not resemble {target}.

I.why: Low sun angles produce long shadows and extreme contrast, which is what polar operations have to cope with.
I.strong: Sun geometry at {site} reproduces the grazing-light conditions of {target}.
I.partial: Low sun for part of the year only.
I.breaks: The sun climbs far higher here than at {target}.

moon: Gravity is 1/6 of Earth's: dust ballistics, slope stability and crew movement all differ.
Hard vacuum, so heat moves only by radiation and conduction, never by air.
No magnetosphere and no atmosphere: cosmic rays and solar particle events hit the surface directly.
Permanently shadowed regions reach 25-40 K; no place on Earth is that cold.
A lunar day lasts about 29.5 Earth days, with two weeks of darkness.
Lunar regolith is sharp, unweathered and agglutinate-rich; Earth soil has been rounded by water and wind.
mars: The atmosphere is about 6 mbar of CO2: enough for dust storms, far too thin to breathe or to carry heat like Earth air.
No global magnetic field, so surface radiation is far higher than anywhere on Earth.
Martian soil contains perchlorate salts, which Earth analog soils generally do not.
earth_side: Earth biology is everywhere, so any site is a contamination source for biosignature tests.
construction_note: Earth gravity means foundation loads, excavation forces and dust settling all differ from 1/6 g or 3/8 g.
No Earth site reproduces vacuum welding, regolith abrasiveness or the thermal cycling a lunar structure sees.
